forces: Soprano, English horn and concert band
performers: Susan Kavinski, soprano; Richard Reed, English horn; United States Navy Concert Band
question: What stays when a song is moved to a different ensemble?
intro: Mahler’s song of withdrawal from the world, played by a wind band rather than his chamber orchestra. The notes here cite his orchestral score for structure and markings only: they cannot show how the band’s unnamed arrangement divides the parts. Listen for the English horn’s opening melody, then for how the soprano restates it and where the music holds back.

sections.label: Stanza 1 · “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen”
Stanza 2 · “Es ist mir auch gar nichts daran gelegen”

cues.title: An English horn opens
cues.text: Mahler marks the opening “Äußerst langsam und zurückhaltend” — extremely slow and restrained — and gives the first melody to a solo English horn. The Navy Band names Richard Reed as its English-horn soloist.
cues.evidence: Full score (IMSLP22552), PDF p. 13 (printed p. 15): “Äußerst langsam und zurückhaltend”, the cor anglais enters pp after a rest in the opening bar. Commons names Reed as the featured English-horn player, and the Universal Edition commentary says the orchestral song begins with a solo English horn: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0333457 . The viewed edition is notated in E♭ major; this recording’s chroma estimates read F major, which may indicate a different pitch from that edition, but the arrangement’s key and any transposition are not confirmed. Report: the file opens at −31.9 dB, reaches −20.6 dB by 0:05, and attack density stays between 0.6 and 1.6 per second to 0:20.

cues.title: Written in August 1901
cues.text: Mahler’s first draft is dated 16 August 1901, at his new villa at Maiernigg on the Wörthersee. It came in his most productive summer, less than six months after a haemorrhage on 24 February had nearly killed him.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition’s account of the Rückert-Lieder dates the first draft to 16 August 1901 at Maiernigg: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596 . Wikipedia’s article, citing Mahler biographies, gives the haemorrhage of 24 February 1901 and the productive summer: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCckert-Lieder

cues.title: The voice takes the tune
cues.text: Around a minute in, the soprano enters, marked “ruhevoll” — peacefully. A commentary on the Universal Edition site says the singer restates and extends the English horn’s melody through the first stanza.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 14 (printed p. 16): rehearsal 1, voice marked “ruhevoll, tranquillo” at “Ich bin der Welt”. The restatement is described on the Universal Edition page cited above. Report: relative level rises from −21.4 dB at 0:55 to −17.3 dB at 1:00 and attack density from 1.4 to 2.2 per second by 1:05; the entry is placed by this rise and by the score’s bar count, not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Time flees
cues.text: At “mit der ich sonst viele Zeit verdorben” — with which I once wasted so much time — Reinhold Kubik hears a “fuga” between voice and bass: offset rhythms that express the loss of time itself, tempus fugit.
cues.evidence: Kubik’s essay on the Universal Edition page cited above identifies the “fuga” between voice and instrumental bass at this line. Full score, PDF p. 15 (printed p. 17): rehearsal 2 “zögernd”, cellos and basses answering the voice. Report: attack density is 6.2 per second at 1:15, 2.0 at 1:20, 4.2 at 1:25 and 5.4 at 1:30, a busier stretch than the introduction. The match to the sung line is by score proportion.

cues.title: The first stanza comes to rest
cues.text: At rehearsal 3 the music slows (“poco rit.”) and returns to tempo for “sie mag wohl glauben, ich sei gestorben!” — it may well believe that I am dead. Mahler adds “Nicht eilen!” — do not hurry.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 16 (printed p. 18): rehearsal 3 “poco rit. a tempo”, the text, then “Nicht eilen! Non affrettare!”. Report: boundary at 1:38 (novelty 0.67); level −22.9 dB at 1:35 and attack density 1.0–1.4 per second at 1:40–1:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Etwas fließender: stanza two
cues.text: At rehearsal 4 the marking is “Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen” — somewhat more flowing, but not hurrying — and the second stanza begins, “Es ist mir auch gar nichts daran gelegen”. The band’s attacks leap to about seven a second.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 17 (printed p. 19): rehearsal 4 “Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen”, harp arpeggios marked mf, strings “ohne Dämpfer”. Report: the strongest boundary is at 1:56 (novelty 1.00); level rises from −15.9 dB at 2:00 to −5.0 dB at 2:05 (the loudest window in the file) and attack density from 3.4 to 7.0 per second. Universal Edition notes the tempo rises slightly in this stanza.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler edits Rückert
cues.text: The poem comes from Rückert’s Liebesfrühling. LiederNet’s checked text records three changes by Mahler: “nichts von mir” for “von mir nichts”, “Weltgetümmel” for “Weltgewimmel”, and “in meinem Himmel” for “in mir und meinem Himmel”.
cues.evidence: LiederNet’s checked German text, with footnotes marking Mahler’s variants, and its attribution to Rückert’s Lyrische Gedichte, Liebesfrühling, Vierter Strauß, no. 29: https://www.lieder.net/lieder/get_text.html?TextId=14001

cues.title: Dead to the world
cues.text: At rehearsal 5, marked “Nicht schleppen” — do not drag — the voice sings “kann auch gar nichts sagen dagegen, denn wirklich bin ich gestorben der Welt”: I cannot deny it; I am truly dead to the world.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 19–20 (printed pp. 21–22): rehearsal 5 “Nicht schleppen”, the text, and “gestorben, gestorben der Welt” with a solo violin “fließend, sciolto”. Report: boundary at 2:54 (novelty 0.87); level −13.4 dB at 2:50 and −16.5 dB at 2:55; D major estimates (r 0.75–0.81) at 2:55–3:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Holding back again
cues.text: At rehearsal 6 Mahler writes “Wieder zurückhaltend” — again holding back — and “Di nuovo ritard.”. In his orchestral score the strings dwindle to ppp; in this band version the level and brightness also fall.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 23): rehearsal 6 “Wieder zurückhaltend / Di nuovo ritard.”, strings “dim.” to ppp. Report: boundary at 3:16 (novelty 0.82); level −15.2 dB at 3:10 and −21.7 dB at 3:20, brightness 1041 Hz at 3:10 and 799 Hz at 3:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tempo I: the world’s tumult
cues.text: “Tempo I” brings back the opening speed for the third stanza, “Ich bin gestorben dem Weltgetümmel” — I am dead to the world’s tumult. The level is low and the key estimates settle on F major.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 23): “Tempo I” and the voice entering on “Ich bin gestorben dem Weltgetümmel”. Report: boundary at 3:36 (novelty 0.78); level −24.6 to −20.0 dB at 3:35–3:45 and F major estimates (r 0.84–0.95). The viewed edition is notated in E♭ and the arrangement’s key is unconfirmed, so the estimates are not used for the harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A tune returns in the Adagietto
cues.text: Reinhold Kubik writes that this song’s motivic material runs through Mahler’s works about love, the Adagietto of the Fifth Symphony among them, “where it dominates the entire closing complex”.
cues.evidence: Kubik’s essay on the Universal Edition page: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0086596 . The Fifth Symphony’s Adagietto is also in this Hall (mahler-5-adagietto).

cues.title: In my heaven
cues.text: At rehearsal 7 — “Ich leb’ allein in meinem Himmel” — I live alone in my heaven — the score says “Ohne Steigerung”, without increase, and the singer is “innig, intimo”. The recording eases from −13.5 dB at 4:10 to −21.4 dB at 4:20.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 22 (printed p. 24): rehearsal 7 “Ohne Steigerung / Senza aumentare”, “innig, intimo”. Report: boundary at 4:12 (novelty 0.52); level −13.5 dB at 4:10, −17.7 dB at 4:15 and −21.4 dB at 4:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song for a small hall
cues.text: Mahler conducted these songs’ first performance on 29 January 1905 in the small Brahms-Saal of the Vienna Musikverein; Friedrich Weidemann sang this one. He wrote that they belong in “small halls”, in a “chamber music tone”.
cues.evidence: The Universal Edition page on the Rückert-Lieder gives the date, hall and Mahler’s remark about small halls: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Rueckert-Lieder/P0032290 . IMSLP’s work page names Friedrich Weidemann as soloist of the first performance, and Wikipedia’s article lists which singer took which song: https://imslp.org/wiki/R%C3%BCckert_Lieder,_GMW_39-43_(Mahler,_Gustav) ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCckert-Lieder

cues.title: A sustained high level
cues.text: Between 4:35 and 4:50 the relative level holds near −11 dB, one of the loudest sustained stretches of the file. In the score this is the repeated “in meinem Lieben, in meinem Lieben” at rehearsal 8.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −13.1 dB at 4:35, −11.6 dB at 4:40, −11.2 dB at 4:45 and −11.6 dB at 4:50, with 4:45 among the five loudest windows in the file; boundaries at 4:38 and 4:42. Full score, PDF p. 22 (printed p. 24): rehearsal 8, “in meinem Lieben, in meinem Lieben”. The match between the passage and the text is by score proportion.

cues.title: In my song
cues.text: The last words, “in meinem Lied” — in my song — come at rehearsal 9, and the sound drops: attacks stop for a moment and the level falls about eight decibels between 4:50 and 4:55.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 23 (printed p. 25): rehearsal 9 “in mei-nem Lied”, voice at p, English horn returning at pp. Report: boundary at 4:56 (novelty 0.59); level −11.6 dB at 4:50 and −20.0 dB at 4:55, a fall of 8.4 dB, and attack density 0.0 per second at 4:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Verklärt: the coda
cues.text: The coda is marked “verklärt, con beatitudine” — transfigured, with blessedness. In the orchestral version, the Universal Edition commentary hears violins and English horn alternating consonance and dissonance, as if gazing beyond the horizon.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 23: violins “verklärt con beatitudine”, English horn in the closing bars. The commentary is on the Universal Edition page for the a cappella arrangement: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Ich-bin-der-Welt-abhanden-gekommen/P0333457 . Report: boundary at 5:20 (novelty 0.63); attack density 0.0–0.6 per second at 5:15–5:30; the placement is by the report and score proportion.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Morendo under a fermata
cues.text: The last direction in Mahler’s orchestral score is “morendo” at ppp, with a fermata on the final chord. In this band recording the level falls from −25.8 dB at 5:45 to −28.3 dB at 5:50, and the file ends soon after.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 23 (printed p. 25): English horn “morendo”, strings “morendo”, fermata, ppp. Report: relative level is −25.8 dB at 5:45, −28.3 dB at 5:50 and −62.8 dB at 5:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The voice takes over the horn’s tune
transitions.how: In Mahler’s orchestral score, after the opening bars of English horn, bassoon, horn and sustained violas, with harp flourishes, the soprano enters at rehearsal 1, marked “ruhevoll” — peacefully. She takes up the English horn’s melody, as the Universal Edition commentary describes, while muted violins, a held clarinet and the low strings (“pp espr.”) support her. No new tempo is marked: the join is made by handing the tune from instrument to voice over a thinner, warmer sound.
transitions.evidence: Full score (IMSLP22552), PDF pp. 13–14 (printed pp. 15–16): the introduction, rehearsal 1, “ruhevoll, tranquillo”, “mit Dämpfer con sord.” in the violins. Report: level −21.4 dB at 0:55 and −17.3 dB at 1:00; attack density 1.4 to 2.2 per second by 1:05. The exact bar of the join is not aligned.

transitions.title: Mutes off; the harp starts to ripple
transitions.how: In Mahler’s score the first stanza closes on “gestorben!” with “Nicht eilen!”, the melody coming to rest over held wind chords. At rehearsal 4 Mahler asks for “Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen” — somewhat more flowing, but not hurrying. The strings play “ohne Dämpfer”, mutes off, and the harp begins rocking arpeggios under the second stanza. The printed key signature does not change; pace, string colour and the new harp pattern carry the join.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 16–17 (printed pp. 18–19): “Nicht eilen!”, rehearsal 4 “Etwas fließender, aber nicht eilen”, “ohne Dämpfer”, harp arpeggios mf. Report: strongest boundary at 1:56 (novelty 1.00), attack density 3.4 to 7.0 per second between 2:00 and 2:05.

transitions.title: Strings fade as the tempo slows
transitions.how: In Mahler’s score the second stanza closes on “denn wirklich bin ich gestorben der Welt” — for I am truly dead to the world — with “gestorben” repeated while a solo violin plays “fließend, sciolto”. At rehearsal 6, marked “Wieder zurückhaltend” and “Di nuovo ritard.”, the strings dwindle to ppp and the harp thins to single notes. The music slows and quietens to prepare the return of the first tempo.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 20–21 (printed pp. 22–23): solo violin “fließend, sciolto”, rehearsal 6 “Wieder zurückhaltend / Di nuovo ritard.”, strings “dim.” and ppp. Report: boundary at 3:16 (novelty 0.82); level −15.2 dB at 3:10 and −21.7 dB at 3:20.

transitions.title: Tempo I returns, low and quiet
transitions.how: In Mahler’s score, “Tempo I” brings back the opening speed at the third stanza, “Ich bin gestorben dem Weltgetümmel”. The voice begins low and quiet over a single harp note while the strings re-enter at pp. After the second stanza’s flowing figures the texture is sparse again. A return of the first tempo, not a new tune, marks the change.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 21 (printed p. 23): “Tempo I”, the voice on “Ich bin gestorben dem Weltgetümmel”, harp and strings at pp. Report: boundary at 3:36 (novelty 0.78); level −24.6 to −20.0 dB at 3:35–3:45 and attack density 0.6–1.8 per second at 3:20–3:40.

transitions.title: The last words, then “verklärt”
transitions.how: In Mahler’s score, after the last words, “in meinem Lied” (rehearsal 9), the voice has finished and the orchestra continues alone. Mahler marks the violins “verklärt, con beatitudine” — transfigured, with blessedness — and the English horn returns for the last bars above sustained strings and harp. The song fades by “morendo” rather than cadencing loudly, and the final chord is held under a fermata at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 23 (printed p. 25): “in mei-nem Lied”, violins “verklärt con beatitudine”, English horn and strings “morendo”, fermata. Report: boundaries at 4:56 and 5:20 (novelty 0.59, 0.63); attack density 0.0 per second at 4:55 and 5:15–5:20; level falls to −62.8 dB by 5:55.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified
fields.note: Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
